mappings.note: Draw the longitudinal-wave diagram (LO-78) and explain particle behaviour (LO-5). The drawing is what separates it from S92, which explains the same physics in words.
Echolocation mechanism described step by step, so LO-77 for analysing how the real-life behaviour works; CG2 for the ultrasound content the frame omits.
Two graphs must be DRAWN (LO-78) to contrast high and low pitch (LO-73) via frequency (LO-6). All three are earned by a distinct part of the task.
Describe an activity (C8.2) that demonstrates sound carrying energy - a claim with no outcome in the frame, hence CG2. Same pairing as O22 and V69, which are the same demonstration at other lengths.
Identify the apparatus from a diagram, state the observation and draw the conclusion: C8.2 for the inquiry, LO-4 for the conclusion.
Definitions of frequency and time period and their reciprocal relation - two of LO-6's listed characteristics.
Mechanical waves are defined by needing a medium (LO-4); the examples asked for are longitudinal and transverse (LO-5). Both halves are required by the marks.
Pitch defined and tied to frequency. Same pair as O33 because LO-73 is the frame's only perception outcome.
Infrasonic and ultrasonic bands plus the audible range: LO-6 for frequency, CG2 for the classification and the hearing limits the frame never states.
Defines an echo (no outcome, hence CG2) and then COMPUTES the 17.2 m minimum distance (LO-79). The computation is what separates it from V79's bare condition.
The slinky is treated as a model of the wave, so C8.1 for the model alongside LO-5 for the compressions and rarefactions - the same reasoning as O17.
Two questions in one: same speed in all media (LO-3's cross-state comparison) and the temperature effect within air (LO-6's speed).
Amplitude defined (LO-6) and connected to perceived loudness (LO-73).
What a tuning fork is (LO-1's named vibrating source) and how its vibration makes sound in the air (LO-2's causal claim).

A claim is put to the student to adjudicate and justify, which is LO-80's reasoning from prior knowledge, on top of LO-4's medium requirement. Not LO-77: no real-life event is analysed for its factors, a statement is judged.
Draw a block diagram of SONAR - a schematic of apparatus, which is C8.1's 'develops accurate and appropriate models' rather than LO-78's data model. CG2 for SONAR itself.
A stated misconception about particle travel must be rejected and justified: LO-5 for the physics, LO-80 for the justification. Pairs with S112, which does the same for LO-4.
Longitudinal versus transverse with examples. LO-5 alone; the frame has one code for this and several items drill it.
Solid versus gas speed with the particle-spacing reason - LO-3's cross-state comparison. Not LO-6: no numeric speed is required.
The flash-before-thunder delay explained by the speed difference: LO-6 for speed, LO-77 for analysing the real event and naming the factor behind it.
Two waves must be DRAWN (LO-78) at equal frequency and unequal amplitude, then judged for loudness (LO-73). The drawing is what distinguishes it from S110's verbal version.
A counterfactual: what if sound did not reflect. LO-80 for hypothesising from prior knowledge; CG2 because reflection itself has no outcome.
Three parts, three codes: describe the experiment (C8.2), name the wave type from the result (LO-4), and draw the labelled apparatus (C8.1).
Echo versus reverberation (CG2), the minimum time and distance computed at 340 m/s (LO-79), and the architect's remedy (LO-75). Each part earns its own code.
Pitch and loudness (LO-73), the quantities they depend on (LO-6), and the audible range with its out-of-range classifications (CG2).
